## AI-Assisted Literature Review

Chapter 2 laid out the 12 steps of a literature review as a human process. This chapter asks a different question of each of those same 12 steps: what does the evidence actually say about how well today's AI tools perform it? The answer is not a single number — it swings from genuinely strong to actively unreliable depending on the step and the type of tool, and this chapter walks through why.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this section you will be able to:

- Distinguish general-purpose "deep research" AI modes from specialized literature-review tools, and explain why their strengths differ
- Summarize what the peer-reviewed evidence says about AI performance at each of the 12 steps of a literature review
- Identify the steps where AI is safe to lean on today, and the steps where it currently fails or lacks evidence altogether
- Recognize recurring failure modes — missed studies, fabricated citations, unstable risk-of-bias judgements, vendor-inflated benchmarks
- Apply a staged approach (deploy now / use with oversight / do not rely on) when deciding where AI belongs in your own review

:::

## Generic AI Tools for Literature Reviews

"Using AI for a literature review" can mean two quite different things in practice, and the evidence behind them looks nothing alike.

- **General-purpose "deep research" modes** — the agentic research features built into general chatbots (e.g. ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research, Claude in agent mode). Given a topic, these plan a search, browse the open web, and synthesize an answer with citations, entirely on their own initiative
- **Specialized literature-review tools** — software built specifically for the review workflow (e.g. Elicit, ASReview, Rayyan, Covidence). These typically combine a machine-learning classifier or active-learning loop with a fixed, curated corpus (Elicit, for instance, searches Semantic Scholar rather than the open web), and are usually designed to slot into one or two specific steps rather than run the whole review

The headline finding across the evidence reviewed in this chapter is consistent: **AI is assistive, not autonomous**. A 2025 methods evaluation across 19 included studies found that generative-AI searching missed a median of 91% of the studies a proper systematic search would have found (Clark et al., 2025) — and the same evaluation concluded plainly that "current evidence does not support GenAI use in evidence synthesis without human involvement or oversight." This is also the position taken by recent field-wide governance guidance — the RAISE recommendations (Thomas et al., 2025) and the joint Cochrane/Campbell/JBI/Collaboration for Environmental Evidence position statement (Flemyng et al., 2025) — both of which require full disclosure of AI use and human accountability for every judgement, echoing the [disclosure guidance in Chapter 1](ch01-chapter-one.qmd#disclosing-ai-use) and the [audit-trail principle in Chapter 2](ch02-chapter-two.qmd#cross-cutting-principles).

Two more caveats are worth keeping in mind while reading the step-by-step evidence below:

- **Vendor figures are not independent evidence.** Tool vendors routinely report accuracy figures in the 94–99% range for their own products; independent, peer-reviewed replications are consistently lower. Both are reported below, but only one of them is peer-reviewed
- **The evidence moves fast.** Most published studies test GPT-3.5, GPT-4/4o, Claude 2, or early versions of Elicit — not necessarily the models available by the time you read this — and reproducibility *across* model versions is itself documented as unreliable (one study found a reliability statistic swing from 0.31 to −0.05 between two runs of the same model)

To keep the step-by-step ratings below comparable, this chapter uses four rough levels: **Strong** (comparable to, or better than, human experts, on solid independent evidence), **Partial** (usable with real limitations, or the evidence is mixed), **Weak** (evidence shows AI clearly underperforming humans), and **Fail** (evidence shows AI unsuitable without heavy human rework). Where no direct evidence exists at all, that is stated explicitly rather than guessed at.

## AI Use Across the 12 Steps

### 1. Question Formulation & Review Type

Asking an AI tool to help refine a research question, or suggest which review type fits it, is one of the most common ways people already use these tools — but it is also one of the least *studied* uses.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini): *"Turn this into a PICO question and suggest whether a systematic, scoping, or narrative review fits best: 'Does mindfulness help PhD students cope with stress?' List the assumptions you're making so I can check them."*
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Strong, but on low direct evidence.** General LLMs are widely reported as good at iterating PICO/PCC/SPIDER framings and suggesting alternative wordings, but no controlled validation study measuring the quality of AI-suggested review questions was located. The rating reflects reasoned opinion and feature description, not a measured benchmark
- **Specialized tools (e.g. Elicit)**: **Partial.** Elicit uses the stated question to suggest eligibility criteria and extraction columns, but offers no guidance on choosing a review-type methodology, and again, no dedicated empirical study exists
- **Bottom line**: teach this step as a genuine evidence gap — useful in practice, unvalidated in the literature

### 2. Checking for Existing Reviews

Before committing months to a review, checking whether one already exists (e.g. in PROSPERO) is meant to be a simple lookup task — exactly the kind of thing AI search should be good at. The one available benchmark suggests otherwise.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: A More Reliable Approach

Given the poor open-search evidence above, skip the chat-window prompt here. Instead, search [PROSPERO](https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/) and [OSF Registries](https://osf.io/registries) directly by keyword, export or paste the results, and *then* ask an LLM: *"Here are the registered/ongoing reviews I found on [topic]. Summarize how each one's scope overlaps with mine: [your PICO]."*
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak-to-partial**, downgraded from a more optimistic baseline rating. Gwon et al. (2024) benchmarked this directly: on a Peyronie's-disease topic with 24 known relevant studies, ChatGPT returned 1,287 "results," of which only 7 (0.5%) were directly relevant, with heavy fabrication among the rest; Bing AI performed better but still returned only ~40% relevant results among 48 hits — both far below what a human benchmark search achieves
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial.** Elicit's own corpus (Semantic Scholar) does not include registries like PROSPERO or OSF, so it cannot natively check registry coverage; this rating, too, rests on reasoned opinion rather than a dedicated study
- **Bottom line**: neither category has been shown to reliably replace a manual registry check

### 3. Protocol Drafting & Registration

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Draft the eligibility criteria section of a PRISMA-P protocol from these notes: [paste your PICO plus inclusion/exclusion notes]. Use the PRISMA-P checklist headings, and flag anything still ambiguous instead of guessing."*
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Assistive only, confirmed.** Models can draft protocol text, but no study has evaluated the *quality* of an AI-drafted protocol
- **Specialized tools**: **Implicit only, confirmed.** A tool's setup page (e.g. Elicit's criteria form) effectively fixes some eligibility criteria as you configure it, but this is not the same as a registered protocol
- **Bottom line**: both ratings are reasoned opinion. This is an evidence gap, not a validated capability — and the protocol is the accountability anchor for the whole review (see [Chapter 2, Step 3](ch02-chapter-two.qmd#protocol-registration)), so it is a poor place to delegate heavily regardless

### 4. Search Strategy Development

This is one of the best-evidenced steps in the whole table, and the evidence is not favorable to general-purpose models.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Translate this research question into a Boolean search string using MeSH terms and free-text synonyms, formatted for PubMed: [question]."* Then, before running it, check every suggested MeSH term against the [NLM MeSH browser](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mesh) by hand — do not trust generated vocabulary terms unverified.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, confirmed.** Wang et al. (2023) found that ChatGPT-generated Boolean queries achieve higher precision but *consistently lower recall* than expert-built baselines — the best single-prompt ChatGPT recall was ≈0.50 against a human-authored baseline of ≈0.83 on the CLEF TAR benchmark. The same study found that **over 55% of the MeSH terms ChatGPT generated were not valid MeSH vocabulary at all**, and — more fundamentally for a reproducible method — that ChatGPT does not reproduce the same search even when given the exact same prompt twice. Staudinger et al. (2024) partially replicated this: LLM precision was higher and reproducible, but recall stayed at or below 0.24 against a 0.832 human baseline, concluding LLM queries are "not suitable for high-recall retrieval" (a 2025 reply, arXiv:2505.07155, disputes this and argues proper query validation closes the gap — a live methodological debate, not a settled one). A 2025 head-to-head in the *Journal of the Korean Medical Library Association* found a professional librarian still beat both Gemini 2.5 (54.7% vs 49.6% sensitivity) and ChatGPT-5 (46.8%) on a real systematic-review topic
- **Specialized tools**: **Weak-to-partial.** Semantic search over a single corpus does not produce an inspectable, reportable Boolean string the way a database search does, and independent recall for tools like Elicit is poor in open search (see Step 5)
- **Bottom line**: do not accept an AI-generated search string unverified — invalid vocabulary terms and non-reproducible output are both documented, peer-reviewed findings, not edge cases

### 5. Running Searches, Grey Literature, and Deduplication

If Step 4 was concerning, Step 5 is where the evidence is most damning for general-purpose tools acting as the primary search engine.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: A More Reliable Approach

This step is a poor fit for a chat prompt at all. Instead: export search results as RIS or BibTeX from each database, and deduplicate with a dedicated tool — Zotero, EndNote, or the built-in deduplication feature in Rayyan or Covidence — rather than asking an LLM to spot duplicates by hand.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak-to-fail, confirmed and strengthened by newer evidence.** Clark et al. (2025) found that across 19 included studies, generative-AI searching missed a **median of 91%** of the studies a real search would have found (range 68–96%). A 2026 orthopaedics comparison found ChatGPT-5 Deep Research achieved 47.5% recall and its Agent Mode 40.9%, against 85.2% for three orthopaedic fellows who spent a combined 268 hours screening 9,101 articles by hand — the AI was much faster (12–14 minutes per search) but missed far more studies. A dental-implantology evaluation found Deep Research sensitivity of only 47.8%, concluding it "can support, but not replace, manual systematic search," and noting it produced some outright fabricated references
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial**, and here the picture is more nuanced. Elicit's search is structured and logged, but limited to its own corpus (Semantic Scholar) plus user uploads. Independent tests found average sensitivity of only 37.9–39.5% against 93.5–94.5% for traditional multi-database searching (Lau & Golder, 2025) — notably, 80.9% of the studies Elicit missed *were* indexed in Semantic Scholar, meaning the shortfall is Elicit's search algorithm, not a corpus-coverage problem. Elicit did find a few studies human searchers missed, and had much higher precision (39.6% vs 7.55%). But when applied to an *already-retrieved* set of records rather than run as an open search, Elicit's title/abstract recall jumped to 90.9% and full-text recall to 100% (BMC Medical Research Methodology, 2026) — the tool performs very differently depending on what job you give it
- **Bottom line**: systematic-review searches are expected to reach ≥90% sensitivity; neither category reaches that as a standalone open search today. Never use a general "deep research" mode as your primary search

### 6. Title/Abstract Screening

This is the most mature and best-validated step for automation in the entire table — but only when the framing is right.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

Set up an active-learning screener like [ASReview](https://asreview.nl/) or [Rayyan](https://www.rayyan.ai/) with your eligibility criteria and a small batch of pre-labeled records, then let it prioritize the rest. To use a general LLM as a *second* screener instead: *"Eligibility criteria: [paste them]. For this title and abstract — [paste it] — answer include / exclude / unsure, and quote the exact phrase that justifies your answer."*
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, reframed to partial.** As an autonomous searcher-*and*-screener, general modes inherit all the Step 5 problems. But used purely as a *classifier* on a record set someone else already retrieved, results look much better: Tran et al. (2024) tested GPT-3.5 across 22,665 citations from five reviews and found sensitivity of 81.1–96.5% (specificity 25.8–80.4%), and it even caught 7 of 708 (1%) citations that human reviewers had missed. Matsui et al. (2024) reported a three-layer GPT-4 method reaching 99.6% specificity, with adjusted sensitivity/specificity of up to 96.2%/99.6%. A 2026 meta-analysis across 18 studies (Xie et al.) found pooled title/abstract sensitivity of 0.92 and specificity of 0.94. Khraisha et al. (2024) is a useful counterweight: accuracy was on par with humans in some tasks, but results were skewed by chance agreement and class imbalance, and non-English extraction sensitivity dropped to just 0.36
- **Specialized tools**: **Strong, confirmed.** Vendor-reported figures claim 94–97% sensitivity, and an independent umbrella-review test found 90.9% recall. Active-learning peers back this up with large, independently-measured workload savings: ASReview reports an average 83% work-saved-over-sampling at 95% recall (range 67–92%); a pharmacy-domain study found 89–90% workload reduction at full recall; a 2026 benchmarking study found 87.2% reduction. Rayyan reports 97–99% sensitivity at its standard exclusion threshold, and 79–100% in a separate vendor-context evaluation
- **Bottom line**: as a second screener on a record set you already trust, both general and specialized tools now have real evidence behind them — this is the step where automation is most defensible today, provided a human remains a screener and a pre-specified stopping rule is used

### 7. Full-Text Screening

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Eligibility criteria: [paste them]. Read this full text and decide include / exclude. If excluding, name the single primary reason from this list: wrong population, wrong intervention, wrong outcome, wrong study design, or not available in full text — and quote the passage that justifies it."*
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, confirmed.** Independent evidence is sparse; the main relevant data point (Khraisha et al., 2024) shows variable sensitivity, again skewed by class imbalance
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial-to-strong.** The same umbrella-review evaluation that tested Elicit's title/abstract screening found full-text recall of 100% (at 62.5% precision); the Xie et al. (2026) meta-analysis found pooled full-text sensitivity and specificity both around 0.99. Vendor claims of 99.5% recall / 70% specificity should be read as vendor-authored, not independent
- **Bottom line**: promising, but with less independent replication than title/abstract screening (Step 6) — treat this as less validated until more independent studies appear

### 8. Data Extraction

Across the whole 12-step process, this is the single **best-evidenced strength** of both categories of AI tool.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM, or as the extraction prompt in Elicit: *"Extract the following fields from this paper and quote the exact sentence and page/section each value comes from: sample size, intervention, comparator, outcome measure, effect size, follow-up duration."* Then check every numeric value against the quoted source by hand — the evidence below shows omissions, not fabrication, are the dominant error here, but numeric fields are still where the risk concentrates.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Partial-to-strong.** From uploaded source PDFs, Gartlehner et al. (2024) found Claude 2 reached 96.3% accuracy across 160 data elements, with 95.0–96.9% test-retest reliability and only 6 errors out of 160 items (mostly omissions, not fabrications). A larger 2025 Gartlehner study across six reviews and 9,341 data elements found AI-assisted (Claude) extraction at 91.0% accuracy, statistically indistinguishable from human-only extraction at 89.0% — and faster and cheaper. GPT-4o has been independently measured at 92.4% accuracy with 94.1% reproducibility, and a Claude structured-prompt approach on 58 Cochrane-style items reached 94.77% accuracy at 88 seconds per trial
- **Specialized tools**: **Strong, confirmed — with the caveat that vendor figures are inflated.** Independent replication (Hilkenmeier et al., 2025) put Elicit at 81.4% accuracy against 86.7% for humans — not a statistically significant difference — and, notably, where Elicit and a human extractor *agreed*, the extracted value was correct 100% of the time (disagreement is where the risk concentrates). Elicit performed worse specifically on non-empirical articles. A separate 2026 study (Lagisz et al.) found 70 of 90 tested prompts exceeded 87% accuracy across seven environmental and life-science reviews. Vendor-reported figures run higher still (94–99% from Elicit's own blog; 99.4% in a VDI/VDE case study) and should be flagged as such. A broader systematic review of 27 LLM extraction studies found accuracy ranging 47–99.9%, with categorical/string data (74–96%) noticeably more reliable than numeric data (47–88%); omissions were the dominant error type (60–74% of errors), and outright hallucination was rare (0.08–6%) — which pushes back on any narrative of "widespread fabrication" specifically for extraction, as opposed to search or citation generation
- **Bottom line**: this is the step to prioritize if you want a defensible, evidence-backed AI use case — provided every field is still verified by a human, especially numeric results

### 9. Quality / Risk-of-Bias Appraisal

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Using the RoB 2 signalling questions, go through this trial domain by domain and quote the passage that supports your answer to each signalling question — don't give a final risk-of-bias judgement, just the supporting evidence."* Keep the actual judgement with a human reviewer; the evidence below shows this is the weakest-agreement step in the whole process.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, confirmed.** Rose et al. (2025) tested ChatGPT-4o against human judgements across 75 Cochrane review–trial pairs and found only 50.7% overall agreement (above chance, but not by much); agreement was much higher on simpler domains like randomization (78.7%) than on the appraisal as a whole. A separate 2025 study found ChatGPT-o3 classified 34% of trials as high-risk versus 22% for a masked expert panel and 12% for the original study authors, with only modest agreement (κ 0.14–0.33). Reliability *within* the same model is also unstable: one study documented a reliability statistic swinging from 0.31 to −0.05 between two runs of the same GPT-4o version on the same domain. The picture improves for simpler, more text-extractive checklists — CLARITY and Newcastle-Ottawa-based tools both report over 85% accuracy — suggesting AI does better where the appraisal criteria are explicit and directly extractable from the text
- **Specialized tools**: **Weak-to-partial.** Elicit's AMSTAR-2 appraisal disagreed with human raters on 24.4% of general items and 30.4% of additional items, with errors clustering on multi-component questions and content buried in supplementary materials
- **Bottom line**: this is where model–human agreement is weakest across the entire 12-step process. Any AI-suggested risk-of-bias judgement must be reported as such and treated as a first-pass flag only, never the final call

### 10. Synthesis & Certainty

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Write a narrative synthesis paragraph grouping these studies by outcome direction and effect size: [paste your extracted-data table]. Flag any studies whose results look inconsistent with the others, and say why."* Have it write and run analysis code for any statistical synthesis, but keep the certainty rating (e.g. GRADE) a human judgement.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Partial, confirmed.** Models can draft narrative synthesis text, and a 2026 study found ChatGPT can approximate some meta-analytic recalculations, but no validated automation exists for GRADE or CINeMA-style certainty rating
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial, confirmed.** Produces a synthesis report, but does not run meta-analysis or apply GRADE; evidence here is limited and largely opinion-based
- **Context worth keeping in mind**: GRADE is used in 89.3% of reviews that assess certainty at all, but only 33.8% of high-impact reviews assess certainty in the first place (Siedler et al., 2025) — and human GRADE agreement is itself imperfect. That imperfect human baseline is exactly why an *unvalidated* AI GRADE rating should not be trusted as a substitute

### 11. Reporting and Citation Accuracy

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

To a general-purpose LLM: *"Check this manuscript draft against the PRISMA 2020 checklist and list any missing items."* Then, separately: *"For each in-text citation in this reference list, tell me whether it resolves to a real DOI."* Treat that second answer as a starting point only — manually verify every single reference against a registry such as [Crossref](https://search.crossref.org/) before submission.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, confirmed** — and this is arguably the most consequential failure mode in the whole chapter. Walters & Wilder (2023) checked 636 citations across 42 topics and found 55% of GPT-3.5's citations and 18% of GPT-4's were **entirely fabricated**; among the citations that were *not* fabricated, 43% (GPT-3.5) and 24% (GPT-4) still contained substantive errors. Chelli et al. (2024) measured hallucination rates of 39.6% for GPT-3.5, 28.6% for GPT-4, and 91.4% for Bard, and found recall of real systematic-review papers of only 11.9–13.7% — concluding these tools are "not recommended … as the primary or exclusive tool" for this step, and that every single reference must be independently verified
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial.** Retrieval-grounded generation (answering from a fixed corpus rather than free generation) measurably reduces fabrication, and some vendors now offer PRISMA 2020 flow-diagram export directly from logged search/screening data
- **Bottom line**: this directly echoes [Chapter 1's guidance on fabrication](ch01-chapter-one.qmd#avoiding-research-misconduct) — verify every reference against a DOI registry before it goes anywhere near a manuscript

### 12. Updating / Living Reviews

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Try It: Example Prompt

Re-run your original saved search string against each database (or use a saved-search alert feature where the database offers one), then ask a general-purpose LLM: *"Compare this new set of records against last year's included-studies list and flag any that look newly eligible against these criteria: [paste them]."* A human still screens every flagged record before it's added.
:::

- **General "deep research" modes**: **Weak, confirmed.** The core limitation is that repeated runs give different results — the same non-reproducibility problem documented in Steps 4 and 9 — which is a serious liability for a process meant to be repeated on a schedule
- **Specialized tools**: **Partial.** Re-runnable in principle, but corpus-limited, and no independent evaluation of living-review performance specifically was located
- **Context worth keeping in mind**: Cochrane's own machine-learning RCT Classifier is an established, validated component used for exactly this kind of ongoing surveillance work — showing that a narrower, purpose-built automation niche can already be trusted where a general-purpose tool cannot

## At a Glance: AI Performance by Step

A condensed recap of every step and both tool categories, for quick reference (see the sections above for the evidence behind each rating):

| # | Step | General "deep research" modes | Specialized tools (e.g. Elicit) |
|---|------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| 1 | Question & review type | Strong (opinion only, no direct evidence) | Partial (opinion only, no direct evidence) |
| 2 | Check existing reviews | Weak-to-partial (0.5% relevant in one benchmark) | Partial (no registry coverage) |
| 3 | Protocol & registration | Assistive only (no evidence) | Implicit only (no evidence) |
| 4 | Search strategy | Weak (recall ~0.24–0.50 vs ~0.83 human) | Weak-to-partial (no inspectable query) |
| 5 | Run searches / dedup | Weak-to-fail (median 91% of studies missed) | Partial (poor open-search recall, strong on pre-retrieved sets) |
| 6 | Title/abstract screening | Weak as searcher, partial-strong as classifier | Strong (workload savings well-replicated) |
| 7 | Full-text screening | Weak (little independent data) | Partial-to-strong (less replicated than step 6) |
| 8 | Data extraction | Partial-to-strong (best-evidenced step overall) | Strong (vendor figures inflated vs independent) |
| 9 | Quality / risk-of-bias appraisal | Weak (50.7% agreement with humans) | Weak-to-partial (24–30% disagreement) |
| 10 | Synthesis & certainty | Partial (no validated GRADE) | Partial (no meta-analysis or GRADE) |
| 11 | Reporting & citations | Weak (18–55% fabricated citations) | Partial (retrieval-grounding reduces fabrication) |
| 12 | Updating / living review | Weak (non-reproducible re-runs) | Partial (corpus-limited, unevaluated) |

## Practical Recommendations

Read together, the evidence above sorts fairly cleanly into three tiers of trust:

- **Safe to deploy now, with human verification** — question refinement (Step 1) and prose drafting (Steps 3, 10, 11); active-learning screeners such as ASReview, Rayyan, or Covidence for title/abstract prioritization, using a validated stopping rule targeting ≥95% recall; an LLM or Elicit as a *second* data extractor working from a human-retrieved PDF set (Step 8), reconciling any disagreements by hand
- **Use only with expert oversight and full disclosure** — LLM or Elicit screening as an assistive *second* reviewer at title/abstract or full-text stage (Steps 6–7), with every false positive and exclusion re-checked; LLM risk-of-bias or AMSTAR ratings as a first-pass flag only, never the final rating (Step 9), given only ~50% agreement with human raters
- **Do not rely on AI for** — using a general "deep research" mode as your primary search (Step 5): a median 91% of relevant studies missed is not a workable error rate; accepting AI-generated Boolean strings or reference lists unverified (Steps 4, 11): invalid vocabulary terms and 18–55% fabricated citations are documented, not hypothetical; treating Elicit search as a substitute for a librarian-built, multi-database search — independent recall of ~38–40% falls well short of the ≥90% a systematic review requires

::: {.callout-note}
## Takeaways

- AI performance is not one number — it varies dramatically by step, from genuinely strong (data extraction, screening a pre-retrieved record set) to actively unsafe (open-ended searching, generating references)
- General-purpose "deep research" modes and specialized review tools have different strengths: general modes are more flexible but far less reliable at systematic search; specialized tools are narrower but better evidenced on the steps they target
- Vendor-reported accuracy figures are consistently higher than independent, peer-reviewed replications — read every benchmark with that gap in mind
- The steps with the strongest evidence (screening, extraction) still require a human to verify every judgement; the steps with the weakest evidence (search, risk-of-bias, citations) should not be run by AI without a human redoing the core work
- Use the staged approach — deploy now, use with oversight, or don't rely on it at all — to decide where AI actually belongs in your own review
:::
